title: How to split bills with a partner or roommate
dek: Compare equal, income-based and room-weighted splits, then agree the payment dates, rounding rules and what happens if someone cannot pay.
metaDescription: Split bills with clear income-ratio arithmetic, room-weighting options, a settlement record and an agreement for changed income or moving out.

paragraphs: Split bills by agreeing what is shared, choosing a method and writing down who transfers how much and when. Equal shares are simple; income-based shares compare ability to pay; room-weighted rent can reflect private space. None is universally fair, and your private agreement does not change what the lease or provider contract requires.

A bill split often breaks down over an assumption rather than a formula: one person thought groceries were shared, another thought an extra parking space was personal, or both thought the other would pay first. Set those boundaries before debating percentages. This guide is for voluntary household agreements, not determining legal responsibility after a dispute.

body.heading: Choose a convention you can both explain
rows: Does equal money leave someone unable to meet essentials?
Each agreed income divided by combined income
Which income basis and review period will you use?
Agreed common-space portion plus private-space weighting
How will size, bathroom and parking differences count?
How will you reconcile changing utility costs?

body.heading: Invented example: keep the full ratio until the end
paragraphs: Suppose two partners agree to use monthly take-home income of $4,200 and $2,100. Combined income is $6,300. Their exact shares are two thirds and one third. For $1,992 of shared bills, the shares are $1,328 and $664. Under an equal split, each would pay $996.

Do not silently replace two thirds with 67%. Using an agreed 67/33 split would produce $1,334.64 and $657.36 instead. Either convention can be chosen, but they are not the same arithmetic. Keep full ratios through calculation, round the final amount to cents, and assign any leftover cent consistently.

Income ratios distribute this example's bill burden in proportion to the selected incomes. They do not capture unpaid care work, disability-related costs, personal obligations or the choice to live in a more expensive home. Discuss those factors explicitly rather than claiming the formula settles fairness.

body.heading: Agree the operating details
items: Name every shared bill and separate personal spending.
Choose the split method and any income basis, period or room weighting.
Calculate shares without premature percentage rounding.
Set a contribution date before each provider payment is due.
Name who makes the provider payment and where confirmation is kept.
Decide how refunds, deposits and one-off purchases will be divided.
Write a shortfall process and a review trigger for income or household changes.
Agree how to settle outstanding balances and shared possessions when someone leaves.

body.heading: Room size is an option, not a fairness law
paragraphs: One roommate convention weights the entire rent by bedroom size. Another splits a chosen common-space portion equally and weights only the remainder by private room size. An ensuite, parking space or an unusually small room may justify a negotiated adjustment. These are agreement options, not legal formulas.

For example, with $2,400 rent, roommates could agree that $1,200 covers shared space equally and $1,200 is allocated by bedroom size. Choosing the common-space portion is itself a negotiation. Utilities may use a different split. Keep the final amounts in writing rather than expecting the measurements to answer every question.

body.heading: Discuss changes before money is missing

items.line: Can we list what counts as shared, compare two splits and choose payment dates before the next bills arrive? I want the agreement to show amounts rather than leave either of us guessing.

I cannot transfer the full amount on our usual date. Can we agree what is covered now, whether any difference is repayable, and when we will review this? We also need to check the provider's deadline.
I do not want to share my full financial details. Can we compare an equal or fixed-amount arrangement that we can both afford instead?

body.heading: A joint account is not required
paragraphs: You can keep separate accounts and use a shared settlement record: bill amount, agreed shares, payer, contribution received and provider payment confirmed. Do not mark a bill paid merely because one roommate sent their share. That transfer and the provider payment are different events.

If using a joint account, ask the bank about access, withdrawals, overdrafts, disputes and closure before opening it. The [CFPB notes](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/can-i-remove-my-spouse-from-our-joint-checking-account-en-1097/) that removing a spouse generally requires consent, subject to law and account terms. Do not assume you can unilaterally remove another owner later.

If discussion involves threats, withheld access to money or coercion, prioritize safety and confidential qualified support over joint budgeting. If a bill is unaffordable or a household member leaves, check the underlying contract and seek local advice where responsibility is disputed. Start the common inventory with a [monthly bills list](/guides/monthly-bills-list).

items.a: Only if both agree it works for their circumstances. Compare the actual amounts and what each person has left for essentials. Income-based or negotiated fixed shares are alternatives, but none automatically accounts for care work, disability costs or other responsibilities. Revisit the agreement when circumstances change.

items.q: Should we use gross or take-home income?
items.a: Use the same clearly defined basis for everyone. Take-home income reflects incoming cash but can be affected by voluntary deductions; gross income leaves tax and benefit differences unresolved. Discuss those differences and choose an agreed method rather than mixing bases or presenting one as universally correct.

items.q: Does our split change what we owe the landlord?
items.a: Not by itself. The lease and applicable law determine obligations to the landlord, while your split records arrangements between household members. Check the actual agreement before assuming you owe only your private share. Obtain local advice if someone leaves or a payment is disputed.

sources.name: CFPB: Removing a spouse from a joint account
sources.note: Verified consent and account-term limitations on removing a joint owner; not a universal account-closing rule.
